_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies". A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn. "cue" is when the talk comes on: "start" as the lesson opens, {"after": "<figure>"} once that figure's task is done, or "check" as the final check opens. "locals" names who in town asked a forecast question, by the forecast's "id" in the lesson file.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. Snow on the Blue Mountains this morning, and frost on the inside of my window. Winter’s here. How’s the basin?

replies.say: Fog. Three days of it, and the fences have grown fur.
replies.back: That fur is rime, and it’s in tonight’s lesson. Don’t touch it; it’s busy.

replies.say: Cold. Ole’s goat is wearing a blanket.
replies.back: And judging you from under it, no doubt.

turns.them: Edna Pruitt has moved the Christmas bazaar out onto the green, because the hall’s being painted, and the Seattle paper says a big rain is coming. And Hap says there’s a cloud like a stack of dinner plates parked over the Blue Mountains, and it won’t move, wind or no wind.

replies.back: Oh, it’s moving plenty. The wind is blowing straight through it. You’ll see.
Edna has never let the calendar tell her anything.

turns.them: This week: the tricks our own country plays. The mountains, the winter fog, and a few rare skies worth staying up for. After this one, you’re trained. I mean it this time.

replies.back: And I was nearly right in August.

turns.them: That’s our lot, living on the dry side. Seattle gets the soaking and we get the leftovers. So how does the air come down to us off the mountains?

replies.say: Warmer and drier, warming at the dry rate.
replies.back: With no cloud left to slow it. That’s why your rain gauge is so lonely.

replies.say: Colder, after the snow on the passes.
replies.back: It’s cold at the crest, but it warms all the way down, at the dry rate. It reaches us warmer and drier.

replies.say: Just as moist as it started.
replies.back: It left its water on the western slopes. It comes down warmer and drier.

turns.them: Which gives Edna’s bazaar a fighting chance. A tent, mind. Not a promise.

replies.say: I’ll tell her the mountains are on her side.
replies.back: Tell her that and she’ll knit them a scarf.

turns.them: That’s Hap’s stack of plates. So why does it sit still over the mountains with the wind blowing forty miles an hour?

replies.say: The wind blows through it. Air turns to cloud in the crest of a wave and dries out behind.
replies.back: Right. The cloud stays put; the air doesn’t. Tell Hap to keep clear of the waves downwind. They’ll shake his fillings loose.

replies.say: The wind can’t reach it up there.
replies.back: The wind is blowing right through it. Air rises into the crest of a standing wave, turns to cloud, and dries out again on the way down. The cloud stays; the air moves.
Not that one. It’s a standing wave: air rises into the crest, condenses, and evaporates again behind. The cloud stays put while the wind blows through.

turns.them: A lens cloud is a rare one. Put it in your journal.

replies.back: Hap will remind you of that until Easter.

turns.them: Photographs done. Now Edna’s bazaar, and then you and I are finished with the workbook. You’re a forecaster, Harrow. I’ll stop calling you tenderfoot.

replies.say: What will you call me then?
replies.back: Harrow. Same as always. But I’ll mean it differently.
Don’t thank me yet. Edna’s bazaar first.
